The page's summary describes a woman to the waist, a serpent tail, serpentine hair, fifty bestial heads of lions, boars, and other animals about the shoulders or waist, a thousand vipers for feet, dark wings, and a scorpion sting raised over the head. The name is glossed as 'crooked' or 'winding.'

Nonnus, quoted on the page, has Zeus destroy her with a thunderbolt. Apollodorus, also cited, only says Zeus slew the jailer and freed the prisoners. The elaborate anatomy is the later poetic picture, and the page notes she may have been identified with Echidna.

sources.title: CAMPE - Theoi Greek Mythology
sources.supports: The Tartarus jailer, Zeus's killing of her, and the composite body in the page summary and in Nonnus.

parodyPotential: A warden made of too many animals, whose only job is to keep the smiths locked up. A thunderbolt is the key, not a new anatomy.
sensitivityNote: A literary jailer. The hundred-animal description is easy to over-design; the job is the interesting part.

name: Empusa (Empousa)
facts: Theoi: the Empusae are daimones who take the form of beautiful women. Behind the illusion, an Empusa has flaming hair and mismatched legs, one of bronze and one of an ass. Aristophanes's Frogs, quoted on the page, has her shift among bull, mule, girl, and dog, with a blazing face and one copper leg.
She is sent by Hecate. Philostratus, cited on the page, says insulting her makes her flee shrieking. The Suda, also cited, derives the name from moving on one leg.

The page also says Lamiae and Empusae lure young men and consume their flesh and blood. That predatory story is not a comedy beat. Mormo, mentioned alongside them, is a bogey used to frighten children, which is also not a beat.

sources.title: EMPUSA - Theoi Greek Mythology
sources.supports: The mismatched legs, the shape-shifting in Frogs, Hecate, and the rout by insult.

parodyPotential: A floor phantom with one metal leg and one that does not match, who leaves if you are rude enough. Do not use the seduction, the blood, or the frightening of children. Hecate is not the target.
sensitivityNote: Medium. The traditional story includes preying on young men and, for Mormo, scaring children. Hecate, who sends the Empusa, is a goddess some people still honor.

name: Cerynitian hind
facts: Theoi: a golden-horned deer sacred to Artemis. Fetching it was one of Heracles's labours. He chased it for a full year and caught it on Mount Artemisium. Artemis objected, and in the page's opening a horn had broken in the struggle. He persuaded her to let him borrow the deer to finish the labour.

The encyclopedia extract says it had golden antlers and brazen feet, and that it had to be brought alive. Callimachus, quoted on the page, says Artemis yoked four of five such deer to her chariot and that Hera let one escape to become the labour.
Some accounts on the page say he wounded it with an arrow. Diodorus lists nets, catching it asleep, or running it down, and stresses that the labour was done by wit rather than force.

sources.title: CERYNITIAN HIND - Theoi Greek Mythology
sources.supports: Sacred to Artemis, golden horns, the year-long chase, and the requirement to bring it alive.

parodyPotential: A quarry the rules say you may not kill, with horns that do not belong to you. Do not make Artemis the joke, and do not break the horn for a laugh.
sensitivityNote: Medium because the hind is sacred to Artemis, a goddess. The animal can be a capture objective. Killing it, or mocking the goddess, is the line.

name: Satyrs
facts: Theoi: satyrs are rustic fertility spirits of the countryside. They consorted with nymphs and were companions of Dionysus, Hermes, Hephaestus, Pan, Rhea-Cybele, and Gaia.
They are depicted as animalistic men with ass's ears, pug noses, receding hairlines, and horses' tails. As Dionysus's companions they drink, dance, play flutes, and sport with maenads.
The page distinguishes subtypes: goat-legged Panes, elderly silens, child satyriskoi, and flute-playing tityroi. Roman tradition identified them with fauns.

sources.title: SATYRS - Theoi Greek Mythology
sources.supports: Fertility spirits, the horse-tail and ass-ear body, and the gods they attend.

parodyPotential: Not recommended as a monster. They are attendants of worshipped gods. A flute-playing extra is the furthest this should go, and Pan himself is off limits.
sensitivityNote: Medium. Daimones in the company of Dionysus, Pan, and other gods. Easy to turn into a crude joke. Prefer not to.

name: Asuras
facts: Britannica's article on the Samudra Manthana calls asuras demons or titans, in an ongoing struggle with the devas. The story is told in the Vishnu Purana and the Bhagavata Purana and is linked to the Kumbh Mela.

In that account the asuras, led by their king Bali, defeat the weakened devas and take the three worlds. The two sides then ally to churn the ocean of milk. The asuras hold the head of the naga Vasuki, who is the churning rope, while the devas hold the tail.

When the amrita appears, Vishnu as Mohini keeps it from the asuras. One asura, Swarbhanu, drinks some anyway and is beheaded; head and body become Rahu and Ketu. Those two are a separate record. Shiva, Vishnu, and the other gods in the story are not targets.

sources.title: Samudra Manthana - Britannica Scholars
sources.supports: Asuras as the rivals of the devas, Bali, the Vasuki rope, and the link to the Kumbh Mela. A different URL titled asura dumped a Rig Veda text and was not used.

parodyPotential: Do not pitch asuras as a generic demon faction. The story is part of living Hindu practice, including the Kumbh Mela.
sensitivityNote: High. A class inside Hindu scripture and a myth tied to one of the largest religious gatherings. 'Demon' is the encyclopedia's gloss, not permission to raid the tradition for enemy types.

name: Rahu and Ketu
facts: Britannica's Samudra Manthana article: the asura Swarbhanu disguised himself as a deva and drank some amrita. Surya and Chandra recognized him. Vishnu beheaded him with the Sudarshana Chakra.
Because he had tasted the amrita, both parts stayed immortal. The severed head is Rahu and the headless body is Ketu. The article says they later became responsible for eclipses.

sources.title: Samudra Manthana - Britannica Scholars
sources.supports: The beheading of Swarbhanu and the eclipse role of Rahu and Ketu.

parodyPotential: Do not pitch a headless eclipse boss from this. Rahu and Ketu are part of Hindu cosmology.
sensitivityNote: High. They explain eclipses inside a living religious cosmology and come out of a myth tied to the Kumbh Mela. Research flag only.
